subject: wendat-laine
title: Why short-lived samples alone give two possible date clusters
creator: Sturt W. Manning and Jennifer Birch; OxCal / IntCal20 models

date.label: Research figure published 2022; models an ancestral village
date.note: Modern research publication, not an ancient object or a new historical entry after 2000. Figure 2 precedes the paper’s additional constraints and preferred later model.

representedDate: Alternative model placements near 1500 or 1600; not continuous occupation across a century
place: Jean-Baptiste Lainé site, Ontario; scientific figure
rights: © The Authors 2022. Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Figure resized and converted to WebP without cropping.
credit: Manning, Sturt W., and Jennifer Birch (2022), A Centennial Ambiguity, Radiocarbon 64(2):279–308, Figure 2. DOI 10.1017/RDC.2022.23. CC BY 4.0. Models use OxCal and IntCal20; original caption identifies input data.
printCredit: Manning and Birch 2022, Figure 2, DOI 10.1017/RDC.2022.23; CC BY 4.0. Resized, no content edits.
alt: Two panels of radiocarbon probability curves. The left groups samples by archaeological phase. The right treats the samples as one phase. Several rows show separate peaks near 1500 and 1600 CE.
caption: These models use short-lived plant samples and illustrate alternative calendar placements. The two groups do not show people occupying the village continuously between them. The paper adds other constraints to prefer a later range; this figure alone is not that final result. Both panels and axes are preserved.
notice: Find the separated groups near 1500 and 1600.
Why would two possible dates differ from a century-long occupation?
relevance: Provides authentic scientific source material for understanding uncertainty rather than decorating a fixed date.
